'''Thomas Harriot''' ({{IPAc-en|'|h|ær|i|ə|t}};<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pronunciation Guide for Mathematics |url=http://ceadserv1.nku.edu/longa/classes/2009fall/mat305/resources/pronunciation.html |access-date=2022-07-17 |website=ceadserv1.nku.edu |archive-date=4 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190904062001/http://ceadserv1.nku.edu/longa/classes/2009fall/mat305/resources/pronunciation.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> {{circa|1560}} – 2 July 1621), also spelled '''Harriott''', '''Hariot''' or '''Heriot''', was an English [[astronomer]], [[mathematician]], [[ethnographer]] and [[translator]] to whom the theory of [[refraction]] is attributed. Thomas Harriot was also recognized for his contributions in navigational techniques,<ref name="Moran2014">{{Cite web|url=https://www.encyclopediavirginia.org/Hariot_Thomas_ca_1560-1621#start_entry|title=Thomas Hariot (ca. 1560–1621)|last=Moran|first=Michael|date=2014|website=Encyclopedia Virginia|access-date=28 November 2018}}</ref> working closely with [[John White (colonist and artist)|John White]] to create advanced maps for navigation.<ref name="Moran2014" /> While Harriot worked extensively on numerous papers on the subjects of astronomy, mathematics and navigation, he remains obscure because he published little of it,<ref name="Chapman2008">{{Cite journal|last=Chapman|first=A.|date=2008|title=Thomas Harriot: the first telescopic astronomer|bibcode=2008JBAA..118..315C|journal=Journal of the British Astronomical Association|volume=118|pages=315–325}}</ref> namely only ''The Briefe and True Report of the New Found Land of Virginia'' (1588).<ref name="Moran2014" /> This book includes descriptions of English settlements and financial issues in Virginia at the time.<ref name="Moran2014" /> He is sometimes credited with the introduction of the [[potato]] to the [[British Isles]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.btinternet.com/~richard.towers/jim/raleigh1.html |title=Sir Walter Raleigh – American colonies |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120526080516/http://www.btinternet.com/~richard.towers/jim/raleigh1.html |archive-date=26 May 2012 |url-status=dead  }}</ref> Harriot invented [[Binary number|binary notation and arithmetic]] several decades before [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]], but this remained unknown until the 1920s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Strickland |first1=Lloyd |author1-link=Lloyd Strickland |date=2023 |title=Why Did Thomas Harriot Invent Binary? |journal=The Mathematical Intelligencer |volume=46 |pages=57–62 |doi=10.1007/s00283-023-10271-9 |doi-access=free }}</ref>  He was also the first person to make a drawing of the [[Moon]] through a telescope, on 5 August 1609, about four months before [[Galileo Galilei]].<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.ras.org.uk/news-and-press/68-news2009/1641-celebrating-thomas-harriot-the-worlds-first-telescopic-astronomer-ras-pn-0947|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130627230355/http://www.ras.org.uk/news-and-press/68-news2009/1641-celebrating-thomas-harriot-the-worlds-first-telescopic-astronomer-ras-pn-0947|archive-date=27 June 2013|title=Celebrating Thomas Harriot, the world's first telescopic astronomer (RAS PN 09/47) |work=Royal Astronomical Society |date=2011 |access-date=4 March 2011}}</ref>{{Sfn|Boyle|2024|pp=183-191}}
[[File:Harriot at Syon Park.JPG|thumb|Thomas Harriot observing the Moon through his telescope from the roof of [[Syon House]] in west London]]After graduating from [[St Mary Hall, Oxford|St Mary Hall]], [[University of Oxford|Oxford]], Harriot travelled to the [[Americas]], accompanying the 1585 expedition to [[Roanoke Colony|Roanoke]] island funded by Sir [[Walter Raleigh]] and led by Sir [[Ralph Lane]]. He learned the [[Carolina Algonquian language]] from two Native Americans, [[Wanchese (chief)|Wanchese]] and [[Manteo (Croatan)|Manteo]], and could translate it, making him a vital member of the expedition. On his return to England, he worked for the [[Henry Percy, 9th Earl of Northumberland|9th Earl of Northumberland]].

==Biography==
===Early life and education===
Born in 1560 in [[Oxford]], [[England]], Thomas Harriot attended [[St Mary Hall, Oxford]]. His name appears in the hall's registry dating from 1577.<ref name=Stedall>Stedall, Jacqueline (2003) ''The Greate Invention of Algebra,'' Oxford University Press. p.3, {{isbn|0-19-852602-4}}.</ref>

Harriot started to study navigation shortly after receiving a bachelor's degree from [[University of Oxford|Oxford University]].<ref name="Chapman2008" /> The study of navigation that Harriot studied concentrated on the idea of the open seas and how to cross to the New World from the Atlantic Ocean.<ref name="Moran2014" /> He used instruments such as the [[astrolabe]] and [[sextant]]s to aid his studies of navigation.<ref name="Moran2014" /> After educating himself by incorporating ideals from his astronomic and nautical studies, Harriot taught other captains his navigational techniques in Raleigh.<ref name="Chapman2008" /> His findings were recorded in the ''Articon'' but were later never found.<ref name="Moran2014" />

===Roanoke===
[[File:English title page, A Briefe and True Report of the Newfound Land of Virginia.JPG|thumb|Title page of ''A Briefe and True Report of the Newfound Land of Virginia'']]
[[File:North carolina algonkin-rituale02.jpg|right|upright=1.3|thumb|Watercolour by [[John White (colonist and artist)|John White]] of [[Roanoke (tribe)|Roanoke]] Indians]]
After his graduation from Oxford in 1580, Harriot was first hired by Sir [[Walter Raleigh]] as a mathematics tutor; he used his knowledge of [[Astrology and astronomy|astronomy/astrology]] to provide navigational expertise, help design Raleigh's ships, and serve as his accountant. Prior to his expedition with Raleigh, Harriot wrote a treatise on navigation.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Jehlen|first1= Myra |first2= Michael |last2=Warner |date=1997|title=The English Literatures of America, 1500–1800|publisher=Routledge|page=64|isbn=0-415-91903-7}}</ref> He made efforts to communicate with [[Manteo (Croatan)|Manteo]] and [[Wanchese (chief)|Wanchese]], two Native Americans who had been brought to England.  Harriot devised a [[Phonetic transcription|phonetic alphabet]] to transcribe their Carolina Algonquian language.

Harriot and Manteo spent many days in one another's company; Harriot interrogated Manteo closely about life in the New World and learned much that was to the advantage of the English settlers.{{sfn|Milton|2000|p=73}} He believed that Indigenous peoples were intelligent but had inferior technology.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Trigger |first1=Bruce |title=Natives and newcomers: Canada's "Heroic Age" reconsidered |date=1986 |publisher=McGill-Queen's Press |isbn=0773561323 |page=15}}</ref> In addition, he perceived Native Americans as having a sense of awe towards European inventions:{{sfn|Milton|2000|p=73}}

{{blockquote|Many things they sawe with us...as mathematical instruments, sea compasses...[and] spring clocks that seemed to goe of themselves – and many other things we had – were so strange unto them, and so farre exceeded their capacities to comprehend the reason and meanes how they should be made and done, that they thought they were rather the works of gods than men.}}

He made only one expedition, around 1585–86, and spent some time in the New World visiting [[Roanoke Island]] off the coast of [[North Carolina]], expanding his knowledge by improving his understanding of the [[Carolina Algonquian]] language. As the only Englishman who had learned Carolina Algonquian prior to the voyage, Harriot was vital to the success of the expedition.{{sfn|Milton|2000|p=89}}

His account of the voyage, named ''A Briefe and True Report of the New Found Land of Virginia'', was published in 1588 (probably written a year before). The ''True Report'' contains an early account of the [[Native Americans in the United States|Native American]] population encountered by the expedition; it proved very influential upon later English explorers and colonists. He wrote: "Whereby it may be hoped, if means of good government be used, that they may in short time be brought to civility and the embracing of true religion."<ref>{{Cite book|last=Hariot|first=Thomas|title=A Brief and True Report of the New Found Land of Virginia (1588)|publisher=University of Nebraska-Lincoln|year=1588}}</ref>  At the same time, his views of Native Americans' industry and capacity to learn were later largely ignored in favor of the parts of the "True Report" about extractable minerals and resources.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}}

As a scientific adviser during the voyage, Harriot was asked by Raleigh to find the most efficient way to stack cannonballs on the deck of the ship. His ensuing theory about the [[close-packing of spheres]] shows a striking resemblance to [[atomism]] and modern atomic theory, which he was later accused of believing. His correspondence about optics with [[Johannes Kepler]], in which he described some of his ideas, later influenced [[Kepler's conjecture]].{{citation needed|date=June 2020}}

===Later years===
Harriot was employed for many years by [[Henry Percy, 9th Earl of Northumberland]], with whom he resided at [[Syon House]], which was run by Henry Percy's cousin [[Thomas Percy (plotter)|Thomas Percy]].{{citation needed|date=June 2020}}

The Duke was surrounded by many scholars and learned men and provided a more stable form of patronage than Raleigh. In 1595 the Duke of Northumberland made property in Durham over to Harriot, moving him up the social ladder into 'the landed gentry'. Not long after the Durham transactions, the Duke gave Harriot the use of one of the houses on the estate at Syon, to work on optics and the [[law of refraction]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Thomas Harriot - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Harriot/ |access-date=2022-11-03 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref>

Harriot's sponsors began to fall from favor: Raleigh was the first, and Harriot's other patron [[Henry Percy, 9th Earl of Northumberland|Henry Percy]], the Earl of Northumberland, was imprisoned in 1605 in connection with the [[Gunpowder Plot]] as he was closely connected to one of the conspirators, [[Thomas Percy (Gunpowder Plot)|Thomas Percy]]. Harriot himself was interrogated and briefly imprisoned but was soon released.<ref name="Moran2014" /> [[Walter Warner]], [[Robert Hues]], [[William Lower (astronomer)|William Lower]], and other scientists were present around the Earl of Northumberland's mansion as they worked for him and assisted in the teaching of the family's children.<ref name=Stedall />

While this was occurring, Harriot continued his work involving mainly astronomy, and in 1607 Harriot used his notes from the observations of [[Halley's Comet]] from [[Ilfracombe]]<ref>{{cite book|contribution-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Dictionary_of_National_Biography_volume_24.djvu/451|title=Dictionary of National Biography, Vol. 24: Hailes–Harriott|title-link=Dictionary of National Biography|editor1-first=Leslie|editor1-last=Stephen|editor2-first=Sidney|editor2-last=Lee|publisher=Macmillan & Co.|year=1890|pages=451–453|contribution=Harriot, Thomas (1560–1621)}}</ref> to elaborate on his understanding of its orbit.<ref name="Moran2014" /> Soon after, in 1609 and 1610 respectively, Harriot turned his attention towards the physical aspects of the Moon and his observations of the first sightings of [[sunspot]]s.<ref name="Chapman2008" />

In early 1609, he bought a "Dutch trunke" (telescope), invented in 1608, and his observations were among the first uses of a telescope for astronomy. Harriot is now credited as the first astronomer to draw an astronomical object after viewing it through a telescope: he drew a map of the [[Moon]] on 5 August 1609 [O.S. 26 July 1609], preceding [[Galileo Galilei|Galileo]] by several months. By 1613, Harriot had created two maps of the whole Moon, with many identifiable features such as lunar craters depicted in their correct relative positions that were not to be improved upon for several decades.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/sci/tech/7827732.stm |first=Christine |last=McGourty|title=English Galileo' maps on display|date= 14 January 2009|work=BBC}}</ref><ref name="VanHelden1995a">{{Cite web |title=Thomas Harriot's Moon Drawings |last=Van Helden |first=Al |work=The Galileo Project |date=1995 |access-date=14 May 2019 |url= http://galileo.rice.edu/sci/harriot_moon.html }}</ref> He also observed [[sunspot]]s in December 1610.<ref name="VanHelden1995b">{{Cite web |title=Thomas Harriot (1560–1621) |last=Van Helden |first=Al |work=The Galileo Project |date=1995 |access-date=14 May 2019 |url= http://galileo.rice.edu/sci/harriot.html }}</ref>

===Death===
From 1614 Harriot was consulting [[Théodore de Mayerne]], who was among [[James I of England|James I]]'s doctors, for an apparent cancer of the left nostril that was gradually eating away the septum<ref>[[H. R. Trevor-Roper]]; Blair Worden, ed., ''Europe's physician: the various life of Sir Theodore de Mayerne'' (New Haven: Yale University Press, 2006) pp. 206-207 and note 1</ref> and was apparently linked to a cancerous ulcer on his lip. This progressed until 1621, when he was living with a friend named Thomas Buckner on [[Threadneedle Street]]. There he died, apparently from [[skin cancer]]. It was suspected that Harriot's cancer was due to excessive tobacco consumption.<ref name="Moran2014" />

He died on 2 July 1621, three days after writing his will (discovered by [[Henry Stevens (bibliographer)|Henry Stevens]]).<ref name="Stevens1900">{{cite book |last= Stevens |first= Henry|author-link=Henry Stevens (bibliographer) |year= 1900 |title= Thomas Hariot, the Mathematician, the Philosopher and the Scholar |publisher= Privately printed at the Chiswick press |place=London  |url=https://archive.org/stream/bub_gb_I2Ua3f2mXooC#page/n5/mode/2up | page =142}}</ref> His executors posthumously published his ''Artis Analyticae Praxis'' on [[algebra]] in 1631; [[Nathaniel Torporley]] was the intended executor of Harriot's wishes, but Walter Warner in the end pulled the book into shape.<ref name="Pycior2006">{{cite book|last=Pycior|first=Helena M.|author-link= Helena Pycior |title=Symbols, Impossible Numbers, and Geometric Entanglements: British Algebra Through the Commentaries on Newton's Universal Arithmetick|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3AnAcnc-yvIC&pg=PA55|year=1997|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-02740-3|pages=55–56}}</ref> It may be a compendium of some of his works but does not represent all that he left unpublished (more than 400 sheets of annotated writing). It is not directed in a way that follows the manuscripts and it fails to give the full significance of Harriot's writings.<ref name=Stedall />

Thomas Harriot was buried in the church of [[St Christopher le Stocks]] in Threadneedle Street, near where he died. The church was subsequently damaged in the [[Great Fire of London]], and demolished in 1781 to enable expansion of the [[Bank of England]].

== Telescope and Moon mapping ==
{{multiple image
<!-- Essential parameters -->| align             = right
| direction         = vertical
| header            = 
| width             = 250
<!-- Image 1 -->| image1            = Harriot moon drawing 1609.jpg
| width1            = 
| alt1              = Moon drawing
| caption1          = Harriot's illustration of the Moon from 1609.
<!-- Image 2 -->| image2            = Harriot Lunar Map.jpg
| width2            = 
| alt2              = Moon map
| caption2          = Harriot's map of the moon from late 1610.
}}
Harriot's 5 August [O.S. 26 July] 1609 drawing of his observation of the Moon has been noted as the first recorded telescopic observation ever made, predating [[Galileo Galilei]]'s 30 November 1609 observation by almost four months.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Pumfrey |first=Stephen |date=2009 |journal=Notes and Records of the Royal Society of London |volume=63 |issue=2 |pages=163–168 |jstor=40647255 |title=Harriot's Maps of the Moon: New Interpretations |doi=10.1098/rsnr.2008.0062 |doi-access= }}</ref><ref name="Bloom2016">{{cite journal|last1=Bloom|first1=Terrie F.|title=Borrowed Perceptions: Harriot's Maps of the Moon|journal=Journal for the History of Astronomy|volume=9|issue=2|year=2016|pages=117–122|issn=0021-8286|doi=10.1177/002182867800900203|s2cid=125625494}}</ref>{{Sfn|Boyle|2024|pp=183-191}} Galileo's drawings, which were the first such observations to be published, contained greater detail such as identifying previously unknown features including mountains and craters.<ref name=":2" /> In a late 1610 drawing Harriot inaccurately drew how far the crescent Moon would be illuminated around its limb, inaccurately drew the position of the craters, and did not draw the relief details that one would see along the Moon's light/dark [[lunar terminator|terminator]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Alexander|first=Amir|date=1998|title=Lunar Maps and Coastal Outlines: Thomas Hariot's Mapping of the Moon|journal=Stud. Hist. Philos. Sci.|volume=29|issue=3|pages=345–368|doi=10.1016/S0039-3681(98)00011-9|bibcode=1998SHPSA..29..345A}}</ref> Critics, such as Terrie Bloom, accused Harriot of plagiarizing depictions directly from Galileo's works and argued that Harriot's representation of the Moon was an inadequate representation that needed to be improved.<ref name=":3" /> However, both descriptions were also deemed valuable due to the scientists focusing on different specific observations.<ref name=":2" /> Galileo describes the arrangement in a topographical way while Harriot used cartographical concepts to illustrate his views of the Moon.<ref name=":2" /> Harriot used a 6X Dutch telescope for his observations of the Moon.<ref name=":2" /> Harriot's recordings and descriptions were very simple with minimal detail causing his sketches to be difficult to analyze by later scientists.<ref name=":3" />  Galileo's astronomical observations regarding the Moon were published in his book ''[[Sidereus Nuncius]]'' in 1610 and Harriot's observations were published in 1784 with some not coming to light until 1965.<ref name=":2" /> Harriot's lack of publication is presumed to be connected to the issues with the Ninth Earl of Northumberland and the [[Gunpowder Plot]].<ref name=":2" /> Harriot was also known to have read and admired the work of Galileo in ''Sidereus Nuncius''. Harriot continued his observations of the Moon until 1612.<ref name=":2" />

== Sunspots ==
Thomas Harriot is recognized as the first person to observe [[sunspots]] in 1610 with the use of a telescope.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Voss|first=David|date=2015|title=March 9, 1611: Dutch astronomer Johannes Fabricius observes sunspots|url=https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/201503/physicshistory.cfm|journal=APS News|volume=24}}</ref> Harriot observed the sunspot with the use of a telescope in a direct and hazardous way.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last=Herr|first=Richard B.|date=1978|title=Solar Rotation Determined from Thomas Harriot's Sunspot Observations of 1611 to 1613|journal=Science |series=New Series|volume=202|issue=4372|pages=1079–1081|jstor=1747843|doi=10.1126/science.202.4372.1079|pmid=17777957|bibcode=1978Sci...202.1079H|s2cid=39401037}}</ref> Even though Harriot observed the Sun directly through his telescope, there were no recorded injuries to his eyes.<ref name="Chapman2008" /> Harriot's depiction of the sunspots were documented in 199 drawings that provided details about the solar rotation and its acceleration.<ref name=":4" /> Like many of Harriot's other notes, depictions of the sunspots were not published.<ref name=":4" /> Similar to the early observation of the Moon, Galileo was also known to contribute his observations of sunspots and published his findings in 1613.<ref name=":1" /> The specifics as to how Harriot's telescope was set up remains largely unknown.<ref name=":4" /> However, it is known that Harriot used different magnifications of telescopes with 10X and 20X power being used most often.<ref name=":4" /> Harriot chose to observe the sunspots after sunrise because it made the vertical easier to analyze.<ref name=":4" /> According to Harriot's notes there was a total of 690 observations of sunspots recorded.<ref name=":4" /> Harriot's findings challenged the idea of the unchanging heavens by explaining the Sun's axial rotation and provided further support for the [[Heliocentrism|heliocentric theory]].<ref name="Chapman2008" />

== Compounding ==
Around 1620, Harriot's unpublished papers include the early basis of [[Compound interest|continuous compounding]].<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal|last=Biggs|first=Norman|date=2013|title=Thomas Harriot on continuous compounding|journal=Journal of the British Society for the History of Mathematics|language=en|volume=28|issue=2|pages=66–74|doi=10.1080/17498430.2013.721331|s2cid=53586313|issn=1749-8430}}</ref> Harriot uses modern mathematical concepts to explain the process behind continuous compounding.<ref name=":7" /> The concept of compounded interest occurs when the more times interest is added within the year assuming the rate stays the same then the final interest will be larger.<ref name=":7" /> Based on this observation, Harriot created mathematical equations that included logarithms and series calculations to illustrate his concepts.<ref name=":7" />

==Legacy==
Harriott also studied [[optics]] and [[refraction]], and discovered [[Snell's law]] 20 years before [[Willebrord Snellius|Snellius]] did; like so many of his works, this remained unpublished. In [[Virginia]] he learned the local [[Algonquian languages|Algonquian]] language, which may have had some effect on his mathematical thinking.{{Citation needed|date=June 2009}} He founded the "English school" of [[algebra]]. Around 1600, he introduced an algebraic symbolism close to modern notation; thus, computation with unknowns became as easy as with numbers.<ref name="KatzParshall2014">{{cite book|last1=Katz|first1=Victor J.|author-link=Victor J. Katz |last2=Parshall|first2=Karen Hunger |author2-link=Karen Parshall |title=Taming the Unknown: A History of Algebra from Antiquity to the Early Twentieth Century|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nQLHAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA248|year=2014|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-1-4008-5052-5|page=248}}</ref> He is also credited with discovering [[Girard's theorem]], although the formula bears Girard's name as he was the first to publish it.<ref>{{cite book|last=Richeson|first=David|date=2008|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LB_6VogerHIC |title=Euler's gem : the polyhedron formula and the birth of topology|publisher= Princeton University Press| page=91|isbn=9780691126777|lccn=2008062108}}</ref>

[[File:Lord Egremont unveils the Plaque to Thomas Harriot (26th July 2009).jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|[[Max Egremont|Lord Egremont]] unveils a plaque commemorating Thomas Harriot at [[Syon House]], West London (July 2009)]]
His algebra book ''Artis Analyticae Praxis''<ref>{{cite book|lccn=43022232|title= Artis analyticae praxis |date = 1631|first =Thomas|last =Harriot}}</ref> (1631) was published posthumously in Latin by his friend and executor Walter Warner. Unfortunately, the editors did not understand much of his reasoning and removed the parts they did not comprehend such as the negative and complex roots of equations. Because of the dispersion of Harriot's writings the full annotated English translation of the ''Praxis'' was not completed until 2007.<ref name="HarriotSeltman2007">{{cite book|last=Harriot|first=Thomas |editor1-first=Muriel |editor1-last=Seltman|editor1-link= Muriel Seltman |editor2-first=Robert |editor2-last=Goulding|title=Thomas Harriot's Artis Analyticae Praxis: An English Translation with Commentary|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fFUrAAAAYAAJ|year=2007|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-0-387-49511-8|lccn=2006938536}}</ref> A more complete manuscript, ''[[De numeris triangularibus et inde de progressionibus arithmeticis: Magisteria magna]]'', was finally published in facsimile form with commentary by [[Janet Beery]] and [[Jackie Stedall]] in 2009.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Schemmel | first = Matthias
 | date = September 2010
 | issue = 3
 | journal = Notes and Records of the Royal Society of London
 | jstor = 20753908
 | pages = 303–304
 | title = Before calculus
 | volume = 64| doi = 10.1098/rsnr.2010.0016
 | s2cid = 202575019
 | doi-access = free
 }}</ref>
Harriot introduced innovations such as symbolic algebra and mathematical notation: he is credited with the first widespread use of the inequality signs "<" and ">".
<ref>{{cite web | title=Artis Analyticae Praxis ad Aequationes Algebraicas Resolvendas | website=Encyclopedia Britannica | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Artis-Analyticae-Praxis-ad-Aequationes-Algebraicas-Resolvendas | access-date=2025-11-30}}</ref>
The first biography of Harriot was written in 1876 by [[Henry Stevens (bibliographer)|Henry Stevens]] of Vermont but not published until 1900<ref name="Stevens1900"/> fourteen years after his death. The publication was limited to 167 copies and so the work was not widely known until 1972 when a reprint edition appeared.<ref name="Stevens1972">{{cite book|last=Stevens|first=Henry |title=Thomas Hariot, the mathematician, the philosopher and the scholar: developed chiefly from dormant materials, with notices of his associates, including biographical and bibliographical disquisitions upon the materials of the history of 'Ould Virginia'|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VOZzvh7GZrwC|year=1972|publisher=B. Franklin|location=New York|orig-year=1900|lccn=72082483}}</ref> Prominent American poet, novelist and biographer [[Muriel Rukeyser]] wrote an extended literary inquiry into the life and significance of Hariot (her preferred spelling), ''The Traces of Thomas Hariot'' (1970, 1971). Interest in Harriot continued to revive with the convening of a symposium at the University of Delaware in April 1971 with the proceedings published by the Oxford University Press in 1974.<ref>{{cite book|title=Thomas Harriot; Renaissance scientist |date=1974|editor-first= John W. |editor-last=Shirley |lccn=74176704|location=Oxford |publisher= Clarendon Press|isbn=0198581408}}</ref> John W. Shirley the editor (1908–1988) went on to publish ''A Sourcebook for the Study of Thomas Harriot''<ref>{{cite book|title=A Sourcebook for the Study of Thomas Harriot|date=1981|first= John W. |last=Shirley |lccn=80002111|location=New York |publisher=Arno Press|isbn=0405138318 }}</ref> and his Harriot biography (1983).<ref>{{cite book|lccn=83003961|title= Thomas Harriot, a Biography |first=John W. |last=Shirley |date=1983|location=Oxford|publisher=Clarendon Press}}</ref> The papers of John Shirley are held in Special Collections at the University of Delaware.<ref>[https://library.udel.edu/static/purl.php?mss0343 Guide to the John Shirley papers related to Thomas Harriot], Special Collections, University of Delaware Library, Newark, Delaware. Retrieved 10 May 2020.</ref>

Harriot's accomplishments remain relatively obscure because he did not publish any of his results and also because many of his manuscripts have been lost; those that survive are in the [[British Museum]] and in the archives of the Percy family at [[Petworth House]] (Sussex) and [[Alnwick Castle]] (Northumberland). He was frequently accused of being an atheist, and it has been suggested that he deliberately refrained from publishing for fear of intensifying such attacks; as the literary historian [[Stephen Greenblatt]] writes "... he preferred life to fame. And who can blame him?"<ref>{{cite book |author=Greenblatt, Stephen |title=The Swerve: How the World Became Modern|year=2011|publisher=W. W. Norton|location=New York|isbn=978-0-393-06447-6|author-mask=1|title-link=The Swerve: How the World Became Modern}}</ref>

[[File:Thomas Harriot Memorial Plaque (Syon Park, London).jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|The Thomas Harriot plaque in the grounds of Syon House (W. London).]]
An event was held at [[Syon House]], West London, to celebrate the 400th anniversary of Harriot's first observations of the Moon on 26 July 2009. This event, Telescope400,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://telescope400.org.uk/|title= Telescope400 – celebrating Thomas Harriot's first ever use of the Telescope in Astronomy}}</ref> included the unveiling of a plaque to commemorate Harriot by [[Max Egremont|Lord Egremont]]. The plaque can now be seen by visitors to Syon House, the location of Harriot's historic observations. His drawing made 400 years earlier is believed to be based on the first observations of the Moon through a telescope. The event (sponsored by the [[Royal Astronomical Society]]) was run as part of the [[International Year of Astronomy]] (IYA).

The [[observatory]] in the campus of the [[College of William & Mary]] is named in Harriot's honor. A [[Harriot (crater)|crater on the Moon]] was named after him in 1970; it is on the Moon's far side and hence unobservable from Earth.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}}

In July 2014 the [[International Astronomical Union]] launched [[NameExoWorlds]], a process for giving proper names to certain exoplanets and their host stars. The process involved public nomination and voting for the new names. In December 2015, the IAU announced the winning name was Harriot for the exoplanet [[55 Cancri Af]]. The winning name was submitted by the Royal Netherlands Association for Meteorology and Astronomy of the [[Netherlands]]. It honors the astronomer.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Approved names 2015 {{!}} IAU100 Name ExoWorlds - An IAU100 Global Event |url=https://nameexoworlds.iau.org/2015approved-names |access-date=2024-11-27 |website=NameExoworlds |language=en}}</ref>

The [[Thomas Harriot College of Arts and Sciences]] at [[East Carolina University]] in [[Greenville, North Carolina|Greenville, NC]] is named in recognition of this Harriot's scientific contributions to the New World such as his work ''A Briefe and True Report of the New Found Land of Virginia''.{{sfn|Milton|2000|p=73}}
